subject: Chemistry
chapter: Classification Of Elements And Periodicity In Properties - Periodic Table

modules.name: Historical Developments and Classification of Elements

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Key Theories, Principles, and Laws

Lavoisier Classification :

  • Classified elements into metals and non-metals.
  • Failed to place metalloids.
Dobereiner's Triads :

  • Arranged elements in a group of three in a manner that the average atomic weight of $1^{st}$ and $3^{rd}$ element is equal to at. wt. of $2^{nd}$ element. For eg. Cl(35.5), Br(81.2), I(127). etc.
  • Drawback: Not all elements can be arranged in triads.
  • Triads are not applicable for d and f-block elements.
Newlands' Law of Octaves :

Arranged elements in order of increasing atomic weight and found that every 8th element shows similar properties w.r.t 1st element.

Drawback: The discovery of inert gases disturbs the position of the eighth element. It is valid up to Ca only.

Lothar Meyer's Curve,:  Plotted a curve between Atomic volume and atomic weight and found that elements having similar properties occupy similar positions on the curve i.e.  :

  • Most electropositive elements i.e. alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs) occupy the peak positions on the curve.
  • Less electropositive elements, such as alkaline earth metals (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba), occupy the descending positions on the curve.
  • The bottom part of the curve is occupied by metalloids (Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te, Po, At) and transition metals.
  • Most electronegative i.e. halogens (F, Cl, Br, I) occupy the ascending positions on the curve.
Based on this curve, Lothar Meyer proposed that the physical properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic weight, which became the basis of Mendeleev's periodic table.

Mendeleev's Table by atomic weights and properties :

Mechanisms and Processes :

  • Arranged all 63 known elements(except noble gases as they were not discovered) in order of increasing atomic weight in 8 groups(vertical columns) and 7 periods(horizontal rows).
  • The groups are further divided into A and B subgroups. A subgroup has normal elements, and the B subgroup has transition elements.
Merits of Mendeleev's Periodic Table:

  • Systematic arrangement of all known elements for the first time.
  • Predicted undiscovered elements using periodic trends and left gaps for those elements in periodic table like eka-silicon (germanium), eka-aluminium (Gallium).
  • Correction of doubtful atomic weights of some elements, i.e. U, Be, In, Au, Pt
Limitations of Mendeleev's Table :

  • The position of Hydrogen was not defined properly.
  • Position of isotopes.
  • Anomalous pair of elements.
  • Like elements were placed in different groups, i.e. Pt and Au.
  • Unlike elements were placed together i.e. K, Rb, Cs and Cu, Ag, Au were placed in a same group.
  • Lanthanides and actinides position were not clear.
  • The cause of periodicity was not clear.

blocks.title: Data
blocks.text:
To identify the ,group of elements are triad  or not

  • First check elements belong to same group or not.
  • Then, arrange them according to their increasing atomic number.
  • The difference in an atomic number of a given atomic number should be the same and either 8,8 or 18,18.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
Identify the set of elements that will form Dobereiner triad.

(1) Lithium, sodium, potassium

(2) Nitrogen, phosphorus, arsenic

(3) Helium, neon, argon

(4) Helium, hydrogen, potassium
blocks.answer:
Option (1)

Solution

(A) Atomic mass of lithium = 7, sodium = 23 and potassium = 39

⟹(7+39)/2 = 23

(B) Atomic mass of helium = 4, neon = 20 and argon = 40

⟹(4+40)/2 = 22

(C) Atomic mass of nitrogen = 14, phosphorus = 31 and arsenic = 75

⟹(14+75)/2 = 44.5

(D) Atomic mass of lithium = 7, calcium = 40 and potassium = 39

⟹(7+39)/2 = 23
In the given options, only the set consisting of lithium, sodium, and potassium is satisfying Dobereiner's triad.

modules.name: Modern Periodic Table and Periodic Law

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Modern Periodic Table

  • Given by Moseley
  • First to draw attention on concept that periodicity depends on atomic number .
  • Ramsay introduced noble gases in periodic table.
Long Form of periodic table / Present form of periodic table

  • Based on Bohr-Bury concept of electronic configuration and atomic number
  • Proposed by Rang & Werner
  • It is having 18 groups (1 to 18) and & periods (1 to 7).
  • Further divided in s, p, d, f blocks depending on last electron filling in whichever sub-shell.

blocks.title: Periods Distribution
blocks.text: Periods 1 to 7 contain 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 elements respectively.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: Identify the element with atomic number 37 and state its group and period.
blocks.answer:
Answer

Period =5, Group = 1

Solution

$\text{Rb: } [\text{Kr}] \, 5s^1$

Period =5 (n=5)

Group number = 18 + given atomic number – atomic number of next noble gas.

= 18+37-54

= 55-54

= 1

modules.name: Screening effect and Effective nuclear charge

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Screening Effect ($\sigma$ ) and Effective Nuclear Charge (Zeff) :

• Valence shell $e^–$ suffer force of attraction due to nucleus and force of repulsion due to inner shell

electrons.

• The decrease in force of attraction on valence $e^–$ due to inner shell $e^-$ is called screening effect or

shielding effect. i.e. total repulsive force is called shielding effect.

• Due to screening effect, valence shell $e^–$ experiences less force of attraction exerted by nucleus. (i.e. net attraction force experienced by valence $e^–$ is called $Z_{eff}$).

• There is a reduction in nuclear charge due to screening effect, that reduced nuclear charge is called effective nuclear charge.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text: $Z_{\text{eff}} = Z - \sigma$

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question:
Which of the following elements will experience the highest effective nuclear charge on its outermost electron?

A) Lithium (Li)
B) Carbon (C)
C) Fluorine (F)
D) Sodium (Na)
blocks.answer:
Answer: C) Fluorine (F)

Explanation: Fluorine has the highest atomic number among these elements ( Li, C ) in the same period (Period 2). As you move across a period, $Z_{\text{eff}}$ generally increases. and generally $Z_{\text{eff}}$ decreases or constant down the group

modules.name: Periodic Trends: Atomic and Ionic Radii

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
• Atomic Radius: Distance from the nucleus to the outer boundary of the surrounding cloud of electrons.
  • Across a Period: Decreases due to increased effective nuclear charge.
  • Down the Group: Increases due to added electron shells.
  • Ionic Radius: The radius of an atom's ion.
  • Cations: Smaller than parent atoms due to electron loss.
  • Anions: Larger than parent atoms due to electron gain.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
$\text {  } \ \mathrm{Z}_{\text {eff }} \propto \frac{\text { Positive charge }}{\text { Negative charge }} $

Atomic size $\propto$ $\frac{1}{z_{eff}}$

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
Arrange the elements in increasing order of atomic radius Na, Rb, K, Mg :–

(1) Na, K, Mg, Rb                    (2) K, Na, Mg, Rb

(3) Mg, Na, K, Rb                    (4) Rb, K, Mg, Na
blocks.answer:
Answer: (3)

Solution:

  • Across a Period: Decreases due to increased effective nuclear charge.
  • Down the Group: Increases due to added electron shells.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question:
The ionic radius of an anion is generally:

A) Smaller than the atomic radius of the neutral atom
B) Larger than the atomic radius of the neutral atom
C) Equal to the atomic radius of the neutral atom
D) Independent of the atomic radius
blocks.answer:
Answer: (B)$$

Solution:

Anions gain electrons, increasing electron-electron repulsion and expanding the radius

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Students sometimes make errors in determining electron configurations, especially for transition metals and their ions.
  • Students often incorrectly compare the ionic radii of different ions without considering their isoelectronic nature.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
The minimum energy required to remove the most loosely bounded outermost shell electron in the ground state from an isolated gaseous atom is known as Ionization energy.

Successive Ionisation Energies

  • $\mathbf{M}_{(\mathrm{g})} + \mathbf{E}_1 \xrightarrow{\mathbf{E}_1} \mathbf{M}^{+}_{(\mathrm{g})} + \mathbf{e}^{-} \quad \mathrm{E}_1$ = Ionisation Energy $I$
  • $\mathbf{M}^{+}_{(\mathrm{g})} + \mathbf{E}_2 \xrightarrow{\mathbf{E}_2} \mathbf{M}^{+2}_{(\mathrm{g})} + \mathbf{e}^{-} \quad \mathrm{E}_2$ = Ionisation Energy $II$
  • $\mathbf{M}^{+2}_{(\mathrm{g})} + \mathbf{E}_3 \xrightarrow{\mathbf{E}_3} \mathbf{M}^{+3}_{(\mathrm{g})} + \mathbf{e}^{-} \quad \mathrm{E}_3$ = Ionisation Energy $III$
  • $\mathbf{E}_1 < \mathbf{E}_2 < \mathbf{E}_3 $ ..... (Always true for an element)

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• First Ionization Energy:
$IE_1 = E(g) \rightarrow E^+(g) + e^-$

• Second Ionization Energy:
$IE_2 = E^+(g) \rightarrow E^{2+}(g) + e^-$

blocks.title: Key Points
blocks.text:
$\text { Ionisation Energy } \propto \mathrm{Z}_{\text {eff }} \propto \frac{\text { Positive charge }}{\text { Negative charge }}$

$\text { Ionisation Energy } \propto \frac{1}{\text { Atomic size }}$

Exceptional Orders of I.E. :

• Check for stable e-configuration, i.e.$s^2$$p^3$etc.

Be > B,   N>O,   Mg>Al,   P>S

• Check for d-block contraction (Transition Contraction)

Ga>Al (only case of d-block contraction)

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
What is the correct order of Ionisation energy?

(1) Al+3 ＞Al+＞ Al+2

(2) Al+ ＞Al+2＞ Al+3

(3) Al+3 ＞Al+2＞ Al+

(4) Al+2 ＞Al+＞ Al+3
blocks.answer:
Ans (1)

$A l^{+3}>A l^{+}>A l^{+2}$

Explanation

$A l^{+}-1 s^2, 2 s^2, 2 p^6, 3 s^2$- Fully filled s-orbital

$A l^{2+}-1 s^2, 2 s^2, 2 p^6, 3 s^1$

$A l^{3+}-1 s^2, 2 s^2, 2 p^6$ - Fully filled shell (more stable)

blocks.question:

(1) Sodium (Na)

(2) Magnesium (Mg)

(3) Aluminum (Al)

(4) Silicon (Si)
blocks.answer:
Answer: (1)

Explanation :

After losing one electron, sodium achieves a stable noble gas configuration, making the second ionization energy very high

  • Start solving IE based question without writing e- configuration.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• Electron Affinity: The amount of energy released when an electron is added to the valence shell of an isolated gaseous atom.
  • Electronegativity: Tendency of an atom to attract a shared pair of electrons in a molecule.
  • Electron gain enthalpy: When an $e^{-}$ is added to a neutral gaseous atom to convert it into a negative ion, the enthalpy change accompanying the process is defined as electron gain enthalpy.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• Pauling Scale for Electronegativity:
$X_A-\chi_B=0.102 \sqrt{\Delta_{A-B}} $ (when energies are expressed in $\mathrm{KJ} / \mathrm{mol}$)
  • Conditions: Based on bond dissociation energies.
  • Limitations: Assumes bond energies are known.

blocks.title: Electronegativity Scale
blocks.text:
Mulliken scale : According to Mulliken electronegativity is average value of ionisation potential and electron affinity of an element,

$\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{\text { Ionisation Potential }+ \text { Electron Affinity }}{2}$

$\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{p}}=\frac{\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{m}}}{2.8}$

$X_p= $  Pauling's EN

$\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{m}}=$ Mulliken's EN

If ionisation potential and electron affinity are given in eV , then electronegativity by Mulliken on Pauling scale will be

$\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{p}}=\frac{\text { Ionisation Potential }+ \text { Electron Affinity }}{5.6}$

If ionisation potential and electron affinity are given in $\mathrm{kcal} / \mathrm{mole}$ then

$\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{p}}=\frac{\text { Ionisation Potential }+ \text { Electron Affinity }}{2 \times 62.5}$

blocks.title: DATA
blocks.text:
Trends:

  • Electron affinity: Increases across a period, decreases down a group. Exceptions: Noble gases, N, P.
  • Electronegativity: Generally increases across a period, decreases down a group.
  • $\text {  Electron affinity } \propto Z_{\text {eff }} \propto \frac{\text { Positive charge }}{\text { Negative charge }}$
  • $\text {  Electron affinity } \propto \frac{1}{\text { Atomic size }}$
  • $\text {  Electronegativity } \propto Z_{\text {eff }} \propto \frac{\text { Positive charge }}{\text { Negative charge }}$
  • $\text {  Electronegativity } \propto \frac{1}{\text { Atomic size }}$
Exceptional Orders of EA:

• Check for stable e-configuration, i.e.
$s^2, p^3, p^6$etc.

Ne<Be<N (The addition of e- in these three will be an endothermic process)

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing electron affinity with ionization energy: Electron affinity involves gaining electrons; ionization energy involves losing electrons.
  • Misinterpreting electronegativity: It is a relative measure, not an absolute quantity.
  • Forgetting exceptions and variations while solving question

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
Which of the following elements has the highest electron affinity?
A. Oxygen (O)

B. Fluorine (F)

C. Chlorine (Cl)

D. Nitrogen (N)
blocks.answer:
Answer: C. Chlorine (Cl)
Explanation:
Although fluorine is more electronegative, chlorine has a higher (more negative) electron affinity due to lower electron-electron repulsion in its larger 3p orbital compared to fluorine’s 2p orbital.
blocks.prompt:

A. Oxygen (O)

B. Fluorine (F)

C. Chlorine (Cl)

D. Nitrogen (N)

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question:
Electron affinity is generally most exothermic for:
A. Noble gases

B. Alkali metals

C. Halogens

D. Alkaline earth metals
blocks.answer:
Answer: C. Halogens

Explanation:
Halogens have a strong tendency to gain electrons to attain a stable noble gas configuration, making their electron affinity highly exothermic.
blocks.prompt:

blocks.title: Example-3
blocks.question:
Q. What is the trend of electronegativity in the periodic table across a period (left to right)?

A. Increases

B. Decreases

C. Remains constant

D. First increases then decreases
blocks.answer:
Answer: A. Increases

Explanation: As you move from left to right in a period, atomic number increases, but the electrons are added to the same energy level. The increasing nuclear charge pulls electrons closer, thereby increasing electronegativity.
blocks.prompt:
Q. What is the trend of electronegativity in the periodic table across a period (left to right)?

A. Increases

B. Decreases

C. Remains constant

D. First increases then decreases

blocks.title: Example-4
blocks.question:
Q. Which group in the periodic table generally has the lowest electronegativity values?

A. Group 1 (Alkali metals)

B. Group 17 (Halogens)

C. Group 16 (Chalcogens)

D. Group 15 (Pnictogens)
blocks.answer:
Answer: A. Group 1 (Alkali metals)

Explanation: Alkali metals (e.g., Li, Na, K) have a low nuclear charge and a strong tendency to lose electrons, resulting in the lowest electronegativity values.
